terms.definition: Domain Name System — the internet's phone book that translates human-readable domain names (google.com) into machine-readable IP addresses (142.250.182.46).
terms.example: Like calling your contact 'Priya' instead of remembering her 10-digit phone number.

terms.definition: AWS's scalable DNS and domain registration service. Acts as an authoritative nameserver. Name comes from Route 66 (US highway) + port 53 (DNS port). Has 100% SLA.
terms.example: Like GoDaddy or Namecheap, but integrated with AWS services and offering intelligent routing policies.

terms.definition: A DNS server managed by your ISP that acts as a middleman — it checks its cache first, then queries root/TLD/authoritative servers if needed. Returns the final IP to your browser.
terms.example: Like a librarian who first checks their own desk drawer, then searches the whole library if needed.

terms.definition: The top of the DNS hierarchy. There are 13 sets globally. They don't have IP addresses for specific domains but know which TLD servers to direct queries to.
terms.example: Like a main reception desk that says 'For .com questions, go to desk B. For .org, go to desk C.'

terms.definition: The last segment of a domain name (.com, .org, .net, .in). TLD servers manage registrations for their extension. .com is managed by VeriSign; .org by PIR.
terms.example: In 'google.com', the TLD is '.com'. In 'amazon.in', the TLD is '.in'.

terms.definition: The final and most important DNS server — it holds the actual DNS records for a domain and provides the definitive answer to DNS queries. Examples: Route 53, GoDaddy, Cloudflare.
terms.example: Like the official address registry — only it has the verified, accurate address information.

terms.definition: A container in Route 53 that stores all DNS records for a specific domain. Analogous to a DNS database. Can be public (internet-facing) or private (VPC-only).
terms.example: Like a folder that contains all the contact information (DNS records) for your company's domain.

terms.definition: A DNS record type that maps a domain name to an IPv4 address. The most common record type.
terms.example: saiguda.info → 54.23.11.45

terms.definition: A DNS record type that maps a domain name to an IPv6 address. AAAA = 4x A, because IPv6 addresses are 4x longer than IPv4.
Canonical Name record — maps one domain name to another domain name (alias). Cannot be used at the zone apex (root domain).
terms.example: fb.com → facebook.com — typing fb.com redirects to facebook.com

terms.definition: Mail Exchange record — specifies the mail servers responsible for accepting email for a domain. Required to enable custom domain email.
terms.example: Adding Google's MX records to use Gmail with your custom domain (info@saiguda.info)

terms.definition: Text record — stores arbitrary text data. Commonly used for domain ownership verification (AWS ACM, Google Search Console) and email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).
terms.example: When ACM asks you to add a TXT record to prove you own your domain.

terms.definition: Name Server record — specifies which servers are authoritative for a domain. Every Route 53 hosted zone automatically gets 4 NS records.
terms.example: The 4 NS values you copy from Route 53 into GoDaddy to redirect DNS management to Route 53.

terms.definition: Start of Authority record — contains administrative metadata about a domain: primary nameserver, admin email, default TTL, and zone serial number. Auto-created by Route 53.
terms.example: Like the title page of a book — who published it, when, and key administrative details.

terms.definition: A Route 53-specific extension that maps a domain name to an AWS resource endpoint (CloudFront, ALB, S3, API Gateway). Works at zone apex, no charge per query, auto-updates.
terms.example: Mapping saiguda.info directly to d1234abcd.cloudfront.net without a CNAME.

terms.definition: Time to Live — the number of seconds a DNS record is cached by recursive resolvers before it must be refreshed from the authoritative nameserver.
terms.example: TTL of 3600 means the DNS answer is cached for 1 hour. After that, resolvers re-query Route 53.

terms.definition: A CloudFront security feature that allows CloudFront to access a private S3 bucket. CloudFront auto-updates the S3 bucket policy so only that distribution can read from the bucket.
terms.example: Like giving CloudFront a special key card to access an otherwise locked S3 storage room.

terms.definition: AWS Certificate Manager — a service that provides free public SSL/TLS certificates for use with CloudFront, ALB, and API Gateway. Certificates for CloudFront must be in us-east-1.
terms.example: The service that gives your website the HTTPS padlock (TLS certificate) for free.

terms.definition: A Route 53 hosted zone that is accessible from the internet. Used for public-facing websites and applications.
terms.example: A hosted zone for saiguda.info that allows anyone on the internet to resolve its DNS records.

terms.definition: A Route 53 hosted zone that is accessible only within specified AWS VPCs. Used for internal services not exposed to the internet.
terms.example: A hosted zone for db.internal.myapp.com accessible only by EC2 instances within a specific VPC.

terms.definition: A Route 53 routing policy that distributes traffic across multiple endpoints based on assigned numerical weights. Used for A/B testing and gradual traffic shifts.
terms.example: Sending 90% of users to the old app version and 10% to the new version during a canary deployment.

terms.definition: A Route 53 routing policy that routes users to the AWS region providing the lowest network latency for their location.
terms.example: A user in Mumbai is routed to ap-south-1; a user in London is routed to eu-west-1.

terms.definition: A Route 53 routing policy that automatically switches traffic to a secondary (standby) resource when the primary resource fails its health check.
terms.example: Primary web server in us-east-1 goes down → Route 53 automatically routes all traffic to backup in us-west-2.

terms.definition: A Route 53 routing policy that routes traffic based on the geographic location (country or continent) of the requesting user — not network latency.
terms.example: Indian users see the Hindi version of a website; US users see the English version.

terms.definition: A company authorized to sell and register domain names (e.g., GoDaddy, Namecheap, Route 53). Registering a domain only establishes ownership — it does not host the website.
terms.example: Buying saiguda.info from GoDaddy is like buying a plot number — you own the name, but you still need to build the house (host the website) elsewhere.
